strengths: SGDRO addresses an important vision problem: maintaining minority-group accuracy under spurious correlations and distribution shifts. The average-loss perturbation followed by a group-robust update is simple, model-agnostic, and described through equations and pseudocode. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b03/review-experiment-albf59fe/call-89360df46360440fae7d6aab807237bc/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The Waterbirds comparison against Group DRO uses matched regularization and five random seeds. SGDRO improves worst-group accuracy from 86.5% to 87.2% and group-average accuracy from 90.4% to 90.6%, with improvements in both minority groups.

Evaluation extends to six DomainBed benchmarks, using three seeds and training-domain validation for model selection. Average accuracy reaches 71.4%, compared with 70.1% for Group DRO and 70.9% for ERM, supporting some usefulness beyond Waterbirds.

Table 2 provides relevant mechanistic evidence: SGDRO reduces both reported Hessian eigenvalues in every group relative to Group DRO under the same regularization. For example, the largest LW eigenvalue decreases from 475.5 to 325.8.
weaknesses: The central guarantees are unsupported. Section 3.1 supplies a local Taylor argument, without a convergence or generalization result. For a fixed group, the implemented update should expand as ∇L_g + ρH_g∇L_S/||∇L_S||, whereas the printed expression uses the overall loss throughout. Correcting this notation still does not establish shared flat minima: a perturbation chosen from the overall loss can miss sharp directions of individual groups. Test-set Hessian measurements provide local curvature evidence, but cannot establish the claimed guarantees.

The distinctive methodological contribution is insufficiently isolated. There is no comparison against SAM applied directly to the group-robust loss, nor an ablation of computing group weights from perturbed versus unperturbed losses. DomainBed also lacks a SAM baseline. Consequently, the experiments do not establish the advantage of this particular coupling over other straightforward combinations of SAM and Group DRO. This missing evidence is consequential given the method's incremental construction.

Table 1 does not substantiate the claimed mitigation of the average-versus-worst-group trade-off. The 0.7-point worst-group improvement accompanies a decrease in weighted average accuracy from 93.8% to 93.1%, and both majority-group accuracies decline. Moreover, the reported LW variations of ±0.7 and ±0.5 are comparable to the gain, and the manuscript does not define these as standard deviations or standard errors. The statistical strength of the improvement remains unclear.

The large differences against ERM and SAM are difficult to interpret mechanistically because their Waterbirds regularization coefficient is 0.0001, versus 1.0 for Group DRO and SGDRO. The matched Group DRO comparison remains informative, but without a regularization ablation, comparisons against SAM provide weaker support for attributing minority-group sharpness differences specifically to the optimization method.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful pseudocode and references to benchmark protocols. The DomainBed perturbation-radius search range, Waterbirds checkpoint-selection procedure, and minibatch group-handling details are not specified. Presentation issues such as the tautological Eq. (2) are readily correctable; the recommendation is driven primarily by the unvalidated design choice and the gap between the central claims and supporting evidence.
